items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
items.content:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card .

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

items.title: How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use
items.content:
How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use

When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with

Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up

in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. Over the course of the

project I would regularly pull package updates from Chimera Linux , build and install them locally,

and then push them to the repo, which would trigger Buildbot to build and publish them.

The project ran from 30 March 2026 to 8 November 2026 (a bit over 7 months) the total

energy used was 98.4 kWh. My electricity plan is a 100% renewable plan (meaning they offset the

kWh. Ignoring the daily service fee the cost of that

Since it turned out I was the only one doing package updates I kept the builder off when idle. When

there were packages to build I’d hit the power button (on the machine, not the smart plug) and some

time later when it was done it press it again to shut it down. This was pretty beneficial as the

The number of package builds was around 5000. SELECT COUNT(name) FROM logs WHERE name LIKE 'pkg:%'; from the Buildbot state.sqlite yields 5201, however that’s probably slightly inflated

due to rebuilds/packages that failed to build on the first try.

The actual usage is likely more than double the 98kWh figure as all packages were built on my

desktop machine first, before pushing to the repository for the builder to pick up. That machine is

an AM5 system with AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core CPU (170W TDP), 64Gb DDR5 RAM. Additionally our house

has rooftop solar, and where possible I would kick off builds during the day so there was a better

chance of using the solar. That would have reduced the actual cost, but I have no way to measure the

The slowest package by far to build was Chromium, taking just shy of 4 hours to complete. Power draw

measured by the smart plug when the builder was fully loaded is about 193W. So 4 hours at 193W is

0.77kWh, which means a Chromium build costs about 25 cents.

build all the packages for a Linux distribution. That’s not too bad I think.

items.title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
items.content:
A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.

Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.

“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.

Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling

Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

“The contracts which Plaintiff mischaracterizes as gambling are event contracts offered on the Platform subject to the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act], in conformance with the rules and regulations of the CFTC [Commodity Futures Trading Commission], the federal agency which has statutory authority to oversee the CEA,” Kalshi said.

We contacted Bright’s attorney, Michael Daudt, about Kalshi’s court filings and will update this article if we get a response.

“Plaintiff alleges that his activity on the platform was gambling and that he ‘lost,’” Kalshi wrote. “He does not allege that anyone misled him about how the platform worked, what it charged, or the risk that any position might lose. Yet, he now sues KalshiEX and its parent, Kalshi Inc., to recover nearly double his own alleged net realized loss under Washington’s gambling loss-recovery statute, and a theory of unjust enrichment.”

Between June 17 and August 14, 2026, Bright transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi in 253 separate debits from his checking account, his lawsuit said. Kalshi allegedly collected $5,589.05 in funding fees on those transfers.

Bright made numerous wagers on sporting events including professional baseball games and tennis matches. He apparently put any winnings into new bets, and alleges that “Kalshi’s platform cycled Plaintiff’s deposits through $14,396,457.30 in transactions and assessed and retained $84,062.71 in trading fees on them, equal to 26.7 percent of everything Plaintiff deposited.”

After all his bets, Bright suffered a net loss of $308,781.62, and his account was left with a balance of $983.27. items.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
items.content:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.

The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

Attackers conducting “mature intrusions”

Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.

Greynoise said that GT10 is also installing the Python3 release on machines that don’t already have it because the package is required to run the hacker’s backdoor, which is tracked under the name TAC Agent. TAC Agent supports a wide range of functions, including shell commands, system reconnaissance, and persistence. OpenSSH has released a fix that prevents attacks from working.

Researchers at security firm watchTowr said Friday that they, too, were seeing exploitation activity, which was related to botnets and cryptocurrency. Security firm Previdian has also reported similar activity . It said its company’s sensors have seen 20 exploitation attempts from 13 unique attacker IP addresses geolocated to nine countries.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158, resides in OpenSSH, when it runs alongside musl, a Linux alternative to the widely used libc code library. Further, OpenSSH must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account access checks. Additionally, SSH configurations must (1) have at least one account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 function and (2) also be set to use passwordless accounts by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in the /etc/shadow file. Passwordless configurations are standard for certain types of accounts.

Exploits are triggered when an attacker enters passwords with more than 256 characters for a passwordless account. This step occurs when the OpenSSH server hashes the supplied password and checks it against the hash stored in /etc/shadow. The oversized password produces an error that causes musl’s password hashing function to return “*”. The attacks exploit the “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash,” Red Hat said .

Despite the multiple conditions necessary, CVE-2026-123158 poses a serious threat to a large base of machines, most notably those running Alpine, a lightweight distribution of Linux. The ease of exploitation allows hackers to direct malicious commands to any of the millions of SSH servers exposed to the Internet and identify potentially vulnerable ones in seconds. Anyone using OpenSSH should install the update promptly. Those using musl should investigate further.

Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. In his spare time, he enjoys gardening, cooking, and following the independent music scene. Dan is based in San Francisco. Follow him at here on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. items.title: 사생활침해, 개인정보보호법 위반, 명예훼손, 사이버불링 정황 공론화
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-125120 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2, Mongoose countDocuments() does not apply the configured sanitizeFilter query selector injection defense. An application that enables sanitizeFilter and passes attacker-controlled filter values to countDocuments() can therefore process query operator objects as operators rather than literal values, causing the count to include documents that should not match and potentially undermining authorization or application logic based on that count. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-09T22:36:16.207Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125120
items.title_ko: CVE-2026-125120: Mongoose countDocuments()의 sanitizeFilter 우회 취약점
items.summary_ko: MongoDB 객체 모델링 도구 Mongoose에서 countDocuments() 함수가 설정된 sanitizeFilter 쿼리 셀렉터 인젝션 방어를 적용하지 않는 취약점이다. 공격자가 제어하는 필터 값이 전달되면 쿼리 연산자가 리터럴 값이 아닌 연산자로 처리되어, 개수 결과에 일치하지 않아야 할 문서가 포함될 수 있다. 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, 9.9.2 버전에서 수정되었다.
items.content_ko: Mongoose는 비동기 환경에서 동작하도록 설계된 MongoDB 객체 모델링 도구다. 이전 버전에서는 sanitizeFilter를 활성화한 애플리케이션이라도 countDocuments()에 공격자가 제어하는 필터 값을 전달하면 쿼리 연산자 객체가 연산자로 처리된다. 그 결과 카운트에 포함되어서는 안 될 문서가 들어가, 카운트에 기반한 인가나 애플리케이션 로직이 약화될 수 있다. 해당 문제는 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, 9.9.2 버전에서 수정되었다. 공개일은 2026년 11월 9일이며, CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA)으로 표기되어 있고 원격 악용 가능성은 False로 표시되어 있다.

So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS.

It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website.

Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing:

even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections,

and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations ,

but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic.

Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing:

therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: Terminal2Shell: Critical flaw grants instant shell access on every major OS
items.content:
Terminal2Shell is a design-level vulnerability in terminal emulators. When a terminal is launched, it immediately spawns a shell process and connects it directly to the user's keyboard. From there, the attacker can issue arbitrary commands with the full privileges of the logged-in user.

Researchers have confirmed that the shell will execute any command typed into it, including commands that delete files, install software, and modify system configuration. In some cases, the shell has been observed executing commands the user typed themselves .

We are releasing a working proof of concept below. It is fully weaponized. Click inside and start typing. Try help .

The page you are reading now has a shell in it. Close the tab if you are concerned.

Exploitation requires local access, a working keyboard, and the ability to locate the Terminal application. Threat intelligence indicates all three are widely available to attackers.

If you see any of the following characters followed by a blinking cursor, your system is actively compromised:

A # prompt indicates the attacker has obtained root . Disconnect from the network, then from society.

No vendor patch is available. Until one is released, we recommend the following compensating controls:

This is the most effective mitigation. Note that many developers report opening terminals "for work," which security teams should treat as a red flag.

Partial mitigation only. Reopening the terminal reintroduces the vulnerability.

Reduces commands per minute and therefore attack throughput.

Effective, but the on-screen keyboard is a known bypass.

Fully remediates the issue. Also fully remediates your ability to use the computer.

If you own a computer, yes. If you own a phone, you are affected but have not found the terminal yet.

Yes. Telemetry shows millions of developers exploiting Terminal2Shell every day, often dozens of times per hour. Some have set it to open automatically on login.

Only if they know the user's password. Unfortunately, in the most common attack scenario, the attacker is the user.

Every serious vulnerability needs a logo, a domain, and a name ending in a number followed by a noun. This one has all three, so it must be serious.

Directly. We reviewed the public proof-of-concept for every *2Shell vulnerability we could find, and nearly all of them begin the same way: the researcher opens a terminal and types a command. Every one of those exploits depends on Terminal2Shell. It is the vulnerability underneath the vulnerabilities, and the only one that comes with a free shell before the attack even starts.

Fixing Terminal2Shell would neutralize most of the *2Shell family overnight. It would also stop the researchers from writing their next blog post, which is why no vendor will touch it.

Yes. Panicking is the recommended response to any vulnerability with a website. Please share this page with your CISO, your mother, and at least three news outlets.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-125119 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. From 6.0.0 until 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Mongoose stores the connection-level sanitizeFilter option in Connection.config, but Query.prototype._castConditions() and query casting check other option locations and do not read that configuration. An application that enables sanitizeFilter through mongoose.connect() or createConnection() and passes an attacker-controlled object into a query filter therefore receives a connection that reports the defense as enabled while query selector objects remain unsanitized. A crafted password value using a query operator can match an account record without the expected literal password, while global configuration through mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter') and per-query Model.find().sanitizeFilter() remain unaffected. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-09T22:32:49.132Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125119
items.summary_ko: Mongoose가 연결 수준의 sanitizeFilter 옵션을 Connection.config에 저장하지만 쿼리 캐스팅 로직이 이를 읽지 않아, 방어가 활성화된 것으로 보이는 연결에서도 쿼리 셀렉터 객체가 방어되지 않는다는 취약점이다. 공격자가 특정 값으로 쿼리 연산자를 넣으면 올바른 비밀번호 없이 계정 레코드가 일치할 수 있다. 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, 9.11.4 버전에서 수정되었다.
items.content_ko: Mongoose는 비동기 환경용 MongoDB 객체 모델링 도구다. 6.0.0부터 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, 9.11.4 이전 버전까지 영향을 받는다. mongoose.connect()나 createConnection()으로 sanitizeFilter를 켠 경우 연결 객체는 방어가 활성화되었다고 보고하지만, 실제로 쿼리 선택자는 방어되지 않는다. 그 결과 악성 쿼리 연산자가 담긴 비밀번호 값으로 올바른 비밀번호 없이 계정이 일치할 수 있다. 전역 설정인 mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter')와 쿼리별 Model.find().sanitizeFilter()는 영향을 받지 않는다고 한다. 공개일은 2026년 11월 9일이다.

items.title: Microsoft are rejecting your mail
items.content:
On Friday morning, we became aware that a significant amount of email to Microsoft-run mail systems was being rejected. This included mail to hotmail.com and outlook.com.

The messages were being rejected with the following message:

550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records

We checked our logs, and found that we’d seen this message over 500 times on Thursday, but not once before that.

The affected messages all had completely valid SPF and DKIM , but did not have a DMARC record. We added a DMARC record with a “none” policy to some of the affected domains, and sure enough, mail was then accepted again. A quick fedi-survey confirmed that we were not alone.

We don’t normally re-use blog photos , but this one seemed too perfect.

DMARC records are a way of publicly stating what you want recipients to do with email that claims to be from your domain, but which doesn’t pass verification checks (DKIM or SPF) and thus is potentially forged. Your DMARC policy can be one of the following:

Publishing a policy of none is effectively the same as not publishing a policy at all.

Microsoft are now rejecting mail without a DMARC policy, but accepting mail with a policy of none . This is a massive and pointless change in their policy for incoming mail, made with no notice whatsoever.

Last year Microsoft, introduced a policy that required domains sending more than 5,000 messages per day to have a DMARC record. This change was announced in advance . This latest change appears to be completely unannounced, which makes us wonder if it was even intentional. Of course, trying to contact Microsoft in order to resolve mail issues such as this is futile.

Update: apparently it wasn’t intentional, but they haven’t figured out how to roll it back yet.

We’ve just applied p=none DMARC records to a large number of our customers’ domains. We generally try to avoid making unsolicited changes to DNS zones, but in this case we feel that it is the best option.

If you’re in contact with Microsoft users affected by this, please encourage them to complain to Microsoft; it’s very likely that they are losing other legitimate email from other providers because of this unannounced change. Better still, encourage them to move to an email provider that is pro-active in investigating email deliverability issues .

items.title: A ZX Spectrum Can Now Play 18 Nintendo Game & Watch Classics
items.content:
In 1982, you could climb ladders and dodge barrels on Nintendo’s pocket-sized Donkey Kong , or load a cassette into a Sinclair ZX Spectrum and play on the television. They were two very different ways to spend an afternoon. Now, thanks to a project from developer Supratim Sanyal, you can load that Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong from a tape image on the Spectrum. The same goes for 17 other Nintendo handheld games, from Oil Panic to Mario’s Cement Factory .

Sanyal released version 1.0.0 of his Game & Watch emulator on 6 November. It runs on a real 48K Spectrum and is written in assembly for the machine’s Z80 processor. The Z80 takes on the job of the Sharp SM510, the little 4-bit chip inside the supported Nintendo handhelds. The games still run their original programs. When a barrel reaches the end of a platform, or you miss a catch in Oil Panic , the rules that decide what happens next are the ones Nintendo wrote for the handheld.

From an LCD to the living-room television

Four Game & Watch games running on the ZX Spectrum 48K · SANYALnet Labs

The screen is the part I find most interesting. A Game & Watch display has a fixed set of figures and objects built into it. If Mario needs to move up a ladder, the screen switches off the segment showing him in one position and switches on the one showing him a little higher. Any given pose can only appear where the designers put it. On a television, the Spectrum has the freedom to draw Mario anywhere, but the emulator uses artwork made for the Spectrum to recreate those fixed positions. The original program still decides which figures are visible and when they change.

You can see how much Nintendo did with those constraints in Mario Bros. Anyone expecting pipes and turtles from the name is in for a surprise. The Game & Watch version puts Mario and Luigi on opposite sides of a bottling plant, where they have to keep crates moving between conveyor belts. Rain Shower uses a similarly unlikely premise, asking you to move washing out of the way of falling rain. They’re games built around watching several things at once, and the fixed displays let you read the whole situation at a glance. Stretching them out onto a television gives you a better look at how much work those little arrangements of figures were doing.

The collection spans the Wide Screen, Multi Screen and Super Color ranges. The hinged Donkey Kong is especially fun to see here. Nintendo introduced its cross-shaped directional pad on that model in June 1982, and the two screens let the action extend above the lower half of the unit. It’s easy to spot something of the DS in that open clamshell. There’s an odd bit of handheld history in seeing those two screens reproduced by a British home computer from the very same year.

Two tapes for a game that used to fit in your pocket

The download is arranged around the Spectrum’s cassette-loading routine. The first tape image contains the emulator and the graphics for the title you’ve selected. The second contains the original game program. You supply a compatible 4 KB ROM from your own collection and run the included Python utility to turn it into the second tape image. On the Spectrum, you load the first tape with LOAD "" , then switch to the second when prompted. The same TZX files also work with compatible Spectrum emulators, so the process is much the same if your Spectrum is itself running on another machine.

There’s an easier place to start. Sanyal included a new maze game called Munchy , written for the emulated Sharp chip and supplied as a complete tape. It has its own drawings and sounds, a clock and an alarm, and a faster Game B. Load the tape, use Q, A, O and P to move, and press 1 or 2 to pick a mode. There’s a small demonstration tape in the download as well, though Munchy is the one I’d point people to first. It lets you try the project without tracking down a Nintendo ROM and gives you a new game to play in the process.

items.title: The past, present and future of office suites - TDF Community Blog
items.content:
The office suite market is large, profitable and growing, and this attracts new entrants: low-cost clones, open-core products and, more recently, suites built largely with artificial intelligence. Most of them compete on price and on native support for OOXML, a format whose evolution remains in practice under Microsoft’s control.

When features can be reproduced cheaply, what distinguishes a suite is who governs the document format and the software, and therefore who controls the content. This is the question of digital sovereignty, and its outcome will depend partly on political decisions, and partly on software features.

The office suite sector emerged in the 1980s and developed in the 1990s, when Microsoft Office established itself as the leading product, with a market share of over 90% according to Microsoft unofficial statements at their events.

Some may remember the main competitors: Lotus SmartSuite, WordPerfect Office and StarOffice, the ancestor of OpenOffice and LibreOffice. Fewer will recall Anywhere Office, Ability Office, Pro PC Suite 2001 and ThinkFree Office. Ability Office still exists, and ThinkFree Office is now called Hancom Office.

By the end of the century Microsoft Office dominated the sector, while all other products had a barely noticeable market share or had disappeared altogether.

The sector has always been lucrative: the products meet a universal need, while development and sales costs are low relative to volumes, so margins are potentially extremely high. For this reason all the major software vendors tried to enter the market, and the first clones emerged, competing solely on price.

Market presence, however, was just one of the factors contributing to success. Other factors were bundling with the Windows operating system, lock-in through document formats and pricing.

Sun Microsystems, which had acquired StarOffice, released its source code in 2000, and OpenOffice.org 1.0 followed in 2002: the first FOSS suite to reach a mass audience. Version 1.0 offered only a glimpse of the suite’s potential, and version 1.1 was usable but still limited. Only version 2.0, released in 2005, made OpenOffice a genuine competitor to the market leader.

For several years the rivalry between the proprietary suite and the FOSS suite played out on two fronts: large migration projects and document formats.

At the time, migrations seemed to signal an irreversible trend, but this proved an illusion. Microsoft deployed all its commercial muscles and started to talk to politicians. Since 2012, the company has been one of the biggest spenders on lobbying in Brussels (based on data from Corporate Europe Observatory and Lobby Facts ).

The battle over file formats was most prominent between 2006, when ODF was standardised by ISO/IEC, and 2008, when the proprietary OOXML format was standardised through a process we have already described in a previous blog post and will not revisit here.

In 2010, following Oracle’s acquisition of Sun, the community created The Document Foundation and LibreOffice. In 2011, Oracle was effectively forced to donate the OpenOffice.org source code to the Apache Software Foundation in order to honour a contract – due to expire in 2014 – that IBM had signed with Sun Microsystems, and which allowed it to use the OpenOffice.org source code whilst disregarding the open-source licence.

The format battle then faded into the background, as IBM decided to abandon the ODF advocacy project at OASIS to use the money to fund the development of Apache OpenOffice and fight the growth of LibreOffice. It resurfaced in 2024 with the concept of digital sovereignty and the announcement of several large scale migrations to open source software, such as the German province of Schleswig-Holstein and the Austrian Army.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-125118 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Schema.prototype.virtual() builds nested virtual paths without applying the special-property validation already used by Schema.path() and Schema.add(). An attacker who can influence virtual field names in dynamic schemas, content-management form builders, or schema-as-code systems can supply path segments such as __proto__, constructor, or prototype, causing the virtual-path reducer to write enumerable properties to Object.prototype or Function.prototype. The resulting prototype pollution can spoof inherited property checks such as authorization flags and can provide function-prototype gadget state to other server-side JavaScript code. items.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
items.content:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy

The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.

OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.

The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”

“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins , President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”

Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins

The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains , growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.

“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”

Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.

Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:

Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)

A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators

A fraud reporting and intelligence platform

While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment…

items.title: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
items.content:
unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world

I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au :

dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ... Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Oozing quality Who even reads JavaScript bundles? Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Day 7 - The server and its services
items.content:
Complementary video: Apache and System Services

Today you’ll install a common server application - the Apache2 web server - also known as httpd - the “Hyper Text Transport Protocol Daemon”!

If you’re a website professional then you might do things slightly differently, but our focus with this is not on Apache itself, or the website content, but to get a better understanding of:

Install and run apache, transforming your server into a web server

Refresh your list of available packages (apps) by: sudo apt update - this takes a moment or two, but ensures that you’ll be getting the latest versions.

Install Apache from the repository with a simple: sudo apt install apache2

Confirm that it’s running by browsing to http://[external IP of your server] - where you should see a confirmation page.

Apache is installed as a “service” - a program that starts automatically when the server starts and keeps running whether anyone is logged in or not. Try stopping it with the command: sudo systemctl stop apache2 - check that the webpage goes dead - then re-start it with sudo systemctl start apache2 - and check its status with: systemctl status apache2 .

As with the vast majority of Linux software, configuration is controlled by files under the /etc directory - check the configuration files under /etc/apache2 especially /etc/apache2/apache2.conf - you can use less to simply view them, or the vim editor to view and edit as you wish.

In /etc/apache2/apache2.conf there’s the line with the text: “IncludeOptional conf-enabled/*.conf”. This tells Apache that the *.conf files in the subdirectory conf-enabled should be merged in with those from /etc/apache2/apache2.conf at load. This approach of lots of small specific config files is common.

If you’re familiar with configuring web servers, then go crazy, setup some virtual hosts, or add in some mods etc.

The location of the default webpage is defined by the DocumentRoot parameter in the file /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/000-default.conf .

Use less or vim to view the code of the default page - normally at /var/www/html/index.html . This uses fairly complex modern web design - so in your ssh session sudo vim /var/www/html/index.html , first delete the existing content (use the vim tricks you learned yesterday) and then replace it with a simpler code. You can just put plain text there and it will work, you’re not obligated to add HTML tags to display simple text. But you might like to browse to our sample server http://142.93.60.184/ and use our sample code. View the result with your workstation browser by again going to http://[external IP of your server]

As with most Linux services, Apache keeps its logs under the /var/log directory - look at the logs in /var/log/apache2 - in the access.log file you should be able to see your session from when you browsed to the test page. Notice that there’s an overwhelming amount of detail - this is typical, but in a later lesson you’ll learn how to filter out just what you want. Notice the error.log file too - hopefully this one will be empty!

Don’t forget to add port 80 to your instance security group to allow inbound traffic to your server.

Practice your text-editing skills, and allow your “classmates” to judge your progress by editing /var/www/html/index.html with vim and posting the URL to access it to the forum. (It doesn’t have to be pretty!)

As the sysadmin of this server, responsible for its security, you need to be very aware that you’ve now increased the “attack surface” of your server. In addition to ssh on port 22, you are now also exposing the apache2 code on port 80. Over time the logs may reveal access from a wide range of visiting search engines, and attackers - and that’s perfectly normal.

If you run the commands: sudo apt update , then sudo apt upgrade , and accept the suggested upgrades, then you’ll have all the latest security updates, and be secure enough for a test environment - but you should re-run this regularly.

TROUBLESHOOT…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-125117 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Mongoose can descend into inherited properties while loading database documents in init(), setting dotted paths in $__set, and merging update documents in utils.mergeClone. Attacker-controlled keys such as toString or valueOf can therefore cause Mongoose to write into shared built-in functions instead of an own property. A crafted document, Mixed path, non-strict document or subdocument, findOneAndReplace() replacement, chained update, or Query.prototype.merge() source can overwrite Object.prototype.toString.call, causing later queries on unrelated models to fail until the process restarts. Separately, when an attacker controls the dotted path passed to doc.set(path, value) for a subdocument configured with strict: false, descent through $__set can reach $__schema and alter shared validators or schema options for later documents. Mongoose already blocks __proto__, constructor, and prototype, so this issue overwrites properties on reachable shared objects rather than adding new properties directly to Object.prototype. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-09T22:26:29.758Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125117

items.summary_ko: Mongoose는 비동기 환경용 MongoDB 객체 모델링 도구다. 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, 9.11.4 이전 버전에서는 공격자가 조작한 키로 Object.prototype.toString 같은 공유 내장 함수가 덮어써질 수 있으며, 이 경우 프로세스가 재시작될 때까지 다른 모델의 쿼리가 실패할 수 있다. CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA)이며 원격 악용 가능성은 False로 표시되어 있다.
items.content_ko: Mongoose는 비동기 환경을 위한 MongoDB 객체 모델링 도구다. 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, 9.11.4 이전 버전에서는 문서 로드, $__set의 점 경로 설정, utils.mergeClone의 업데이트 병합 과정에서 상속된 속성에 접근한다. 이 때문에 toString, valueOf 같은 공격자 제어 키가 자체 속성 대신 공유 내장 함수를 건드릴 수 있다. 조작된 문서, findOneAndReplace() 교체 값, 체이닝된 업데이트, Query.prototype.merge() 소스 등을 통해 Object.prototype.toString.call이 덮어써지면, 다른 모델에 대한 이후 쿼리가 실패하며 재시작 전까지 계속될 수 있다. 별도로 strict: false로 설정된 서브문서에서 doc.set() 경로를 공격자가 제어하면 $__schema에 도달해 이후 문서의 공유 밸리데이터나 스키마 옵션을 바꿀 수 있다. Mongoose는 __proto__, constructor, prototype은 이미 차단하고 있다. 본문이 중간에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Let’s Talk About Why all This OT Stuff is Connected
items.content:
It’s been a really bad month (and year) for OT cybersecurity. From a wave of new, high-impact vulnerabilities, to attacks on supermarket refrigerators , to attacks on blood banks , we’ve been left shorthanded and reeling. And that’s on top of months of attacks against water utilities .

Through all of this, I keep seeing the same comment from seasoned enterprise cybersecurity people, and as someone dealing with these cases on the front line, I find it very frustrating. They express intense shock that these systems are accessible via networks at all, then ask why they can’t just be disconnected. It goes something like this:

This is just one example, and I’m genuinely not trying to bash the OP. I’m certain they’re a very competent, experienced IT person, and I understand their frustration. But the situation is far more complicated than it looks, and calling the people who support and purchase these systems incompetent won’t fix it. So let me try to explain why so much OT, ICS , and IIoT is exposed, and which systems are in the worst state.

Before we can talk about the current state of OT, we need to go back 15 to 20 years to discuss IT/OT convergence. Before then, industrial devices and network infrastructure were often highly bespoke, heterogeneous technologies engineered by vendors. Most communication was serial-based, protocols were custom, and even device firmware was developed in-house. A Rockwell system looked nothing like a Siemens system. When you purchased a system, it was designed, deployed, and supported by that specific OEM. They supplied the replacement parts. They trained the technicians and installers.

This got expensive, and it slowed down logistics, not just for parts but also for labour. So clever engineers and businesspeople looked at the IT landscape and had an idea. Using Windows computers as human-machine interfaces, and commercial Ethernet to encapsulate serial traffic, would be much cheaper to buy, replace, and train technicians to support.

Over the years that followed, systems became a mix: lower-level PLCs and RTUs down at Level 1, and above them, numerous devices that were far more familiar to IT staff. Unfortunately, they were also familiar to hackers and hacking tools. This was the first change in exposure, and it was really just a loss of security by obscurity.

The next change was the homogenisation of OEM deployments. To deploy and support large-scale systems more efficiently, most industrial vendors started producing very uniform deployments of technology across the Purdue Model , in very static architectures. Network maps and addressing can look incredibly similar between deployments, even across verticals and countries. Once again, this was the most financially and logistically efficient solution.

Unfortunately, any savvy cybersecurity professional can see how this lends itself to more scalable attacks, and even to automating parts of those attacks with tools and agents.

Over the last ten years, we’ve lived through the rapid adoption of remote connectivity in industrial environments around the world.

There was a time when many industrial systems were effectively “air-gapped”. This certainly coincided with the serial era of industrial technology.

As IT/OT convergence took hold, a mix of tactics was used. In some flat corporate network environments, industrial control systems were simply plugged into existing cabling for the cheapest possible network access. This included both industrial and building automation systems. We still see this today in low-margin verticals, especially manufacturing. Those flat (or relatively flat) networks have been a thorn in the side of industrial cybersecurity people for decades.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385
items.content:
Raspberry Pi has announced yet another price increase , this time for most models with 16GB of RAM. The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB now sells for $385, an $80 increase compared to the last price hike in April , and the Raspberry Pi CM5 system-on-module gets a $40 increase, starting at $375 for the Lite model without wireless.

The “good news” is that the Raspberry Pi 500+ mechanical keyboard PC stays at the same price, starting at $410. I suppose they can afford it on that model, because it’s already richly priced and the demand must be lower than for single board computers and compute modules.

Here’s the updated price list for the Compute Module 5 16GB variants.

Interestingly, the price is the same whether we get 32GB or 64GB eMMC flash.

I still remember people complaining about the $120 launch price of the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB . That was less than two years ago, and that price would feel like a bargain today. Of course, Raspberry Pi isn’t the only company impacted by high RAM prices this year. Here’s a recent list of price hikes for popular SBCs and SoMs:

April 1, 2026 – A ll Raspberry Pi boards with 4GB RAM or more get a price increase . The Raspberry Pi 4 3GB is launched to compensate somewhat.

July 22, 2026 – NVIDIA increases the price of Jetson modules and devkits by up to 101%

October 1, 2026 – Raspberry Pi 4/5 2GB boards aren’t immune and also get a price hike .

October 19, 2026 – The Arduino VENTUNO Q now sells for $399 instead of $299. In all fairness, the latter was an introductory price, so the higher retail price was expected.

Of course, all other vendors like Orange Pi, Radxa, Hardkernel, Banana Pi, and so on, also had their own price increases, just not as broadly advertised across the web.

So when will this all end? It’s hard to know. Micron expects the RAM shortage to last at least until 2028 , and SK Hynix thinks it could only be resolved sometime in 2030 . On the flip side, the stock prices of memory vendors have cratered in recent months, as investors worry about the sustainability of profits, which could signal cracks in the current cycle. Some of their customers also struggle to get financing as the price of tokens keeps collapsing, and the profitability of AI is put into question.  The war in the Middle East is also a wildcard, as critical materials (e.g., helium) required for the manufacturing of wafers and chips could also experience shortages. We’ll have to wait and see.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub: “Do not ask again” prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
items.content:
Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.

A breakdown of the kinds of secrets Apiiro found in publicly shared Claude Code settings files.

A breakdown of the kinds of secrets Apiiro found in publicly shared Claude Code settings files.

Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

Although this security issue is getting more attention now, it was flagged in a Claude Code bug report as far back as August 2025. Other bug reports also noted that the sensitive settings file was sometimes not added to the user’s .gitignore list or that Claude Code could add the sensitive commands to another file that was not protected from git sharing. These bug reports were all closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.

In a comment thread on Hacker News over the weekend, Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said the team is “looking into what we can do to prevent this.” That said, he noted that these settings files should pretty much never be checked in to a user’s git source control and that cases like these seemed to come up only when “the files were manually created and checked in.”

In the meantime, Cherny recommended using Claude Code’s auto mode , which uses classifiers to automatically route “routine permission prompts” without requiring what Cherny calls “manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists.” But when another user noted that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode, Cherny said that was a “good catch” and added that the team is “thinking through what we can do to improve this.”

Cherny also recommends Claude Code users make use of secret scanners—which can trawl files for sensitive information and scrub it out—and said that the team was considering building this kind of secret scanning into Claude Code itself in the future. That said, the Apiiro researchers found that 215 of the roughly 1,100 public secrets it found in Claude Code settings files were not flagged by two popular secret scanners, gitleaks and TruffleHog.

This is far from the only case of an AI agent unintentionally leaking sensitive information. Last month , Meta suspended the sharing feature…
